subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul: look-alike vowels
title: Junho reads the shop labels aloud
goal: Find the readings in a classmate's list that mix up look-alike vowels, name the kind of mistake, and write the correct readings.
thinking: Checking a reading letter by letter
Naming the pattern behind an error
Correcting with a memory tip
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a word. Here you check someone else's reading, find every wrong line, and say what kind of mistake it is.
prerequisites: Knows the Hangul letters and their basic sounds
material: Junho is learning Hangul. He reads six labels from a shop aloud and writes his readings next to the words. Letter values to use: ㅏ = a, ㅓ = eo (like 'uh'), ㅗ = o, ㅜ = u, ㅣ = i, ㅡ = eu; ㄱ = g, ㄴ = n, ㄷ = d, ㅁ = m, ㅂ = b, ㄹ = r/l; a block starting with ㅇ starts with a vowel sound. Some of Junho's readings are wrong.

steps.prompt: Pick one line where Junho's reading does not match the Hangul. (More than one line is wrong.)
steps.explain: Lines 2 and 4 are wrong. 구두 has ㅜ (u), so it is gu-du, not go-du. 거미 has ㅓ (eo), so it is geo-mi, not ga-mi. The other four lines match.
hints: Read each block yourself with the letter values, then compare your reading with Junho's.
Compare the vowel in each block with the vowel in his reading, one block at a time.

steps.prompt: What kind of mistake is it?

options.text: He mixed up two similar consonants (for example ㄱ and ㅋ).
options.reveals: The consonants in the wrong lines (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅁ) were read correctly (g, d, m). The change is in the vowel.

options.text: He mixed up vowels that look alike: the stroke is on the other side or the other end (ㅜ/ㅗ, ㅓ/ㅏ).
He read the blocks in the wrong order, last block first.
options.reveals: Both readings keep the order of the blocks (go-du has the same order as gu-du). Only a vowel sound changed.

options.text: He forgot that ㅇ at the start of a block makes no sound.
options.reveals: The words with a starting ㅇ (우유) were read correctly, and the wrong lines have no starting ㅇ.

steps.explain: In both wrong lines the vowel changed: ㅜ became o, and ㅓ became a. These pairs differ only in where the short stroke sits. Look-alike vowels are a common first mistake.
hints: List which letters changed between the Hangul and Junho's reading in each wrong line.
Is the change in a consonant, in a vowel, or in the order of the blocks?

steps.prompt: Write the correct reading of the two wrong words in Latin letters (like 'na-mu'), then add one short tip that helps Junho tell the look-alike vowels apart.

checks.label: gives the correct reading of 구두 (gu-du)
gives the correct reading of 거미 (geo-mi)
adds a tip about the stroke (position, side, direction, up/down)

selfAssess: Is each reading made only from the letter values given?
Does my tip say where the stroke of each vowel is?

modelAnswers.text: gu-du and geo-mi. Tip: ㅜ has its stroke below the line, ㅗ has it above.
구두 = gudu, 거미 = geomi. Tip: for ㅓ the short stroke points to the left side, for ㅏ it is on the right.
gu-du / geo-mi. Remember: 'up' vowel ㅗ is o, 'down' vowel ㅜ is u.

badAnswers.why: These are Junho's wrong readings again; no tip.
The readings are right, but there is no tip about telling the vowels apart.

steps.humanReview: Whether the memory tip is clear and true for the vowels in question; other tips (a picture, a rhyme) can be fine.
hints: Compare your own reading of the two wrong words block by block.
The tip should say where the short stroke is (above, below, left or right of the long line).

rubric.full: Picks a wrong line and sees that the other wrong line has the same kind of problem
rubric.partial: Picks a wrong line but cannot say what is wrong in it

rubric.full: Names the vowel mix-up, gives both correct readings and a usable tip
rubric.partial: One correct reading or no tip

alternatives: Readings such as 'kudu' or 'keomi' (k for g) follow another romanization habit and are accepted.
A tip that uses a picture or a rhyme instead of a rule about strokes is fine if it is correct.
hardCases: Real learners often confuse ㅓ with ㅗ as well; a mistake in a different pair is still a vowel mix-up.

cautions.language: All Korean texts are single words or very short phrases. Latin-letter readings follow common revised romanization; other spellings of the same sound (for example k for g) are accepted.
cautions.culture: Korean letter shapes and their sounds are fixed, but romanization is only a tool; Latin readings differ between systems and never replace hearing the sound.
cautions.accessibility: All words are shown in text with their meaning in English; no sound or picture is needed. Letters are described by shape and position, not by colour.

auto: Picking a wrong line
Choice about the kind of mistake
Both correct Latin-letter readings present and a tip about stroke position present
human: Whether the tip is helpful and true

subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul: the final consonant (받침) changes the word
title: Is the small bottom letter just decoration?
goal: Judge a classmate's claim about the final consonant (받침) with evidence from a price tag and a payment, and explain it in your own words.
thinking: Testing a claim against evidence
Seeing that a small detail can change the meaning
Explaining a reading rule to someone
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read 삼천 원 aloud. Here you decide whether a classmate's rule about the bottom letter holds, and prove it with evidence outside the tag.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul blocks with a final consonant
Knows the numbers 이, 삼, 사, 오 and 천
material: At a market stall, Jiwoo and Hajun look at the price tag on a bag of apples. Numbers you need: 이 = 2, 삼 = 3, 사 = 4, 오 = 5, 천 = 1,000 (so 이천 원 = 2,000 won). Jiwoo reads the tag as 삼천 원. Hajun says: 'The little letter at the bottom of a block is only decoration, so 삼 and 사 are the same and I read 사천 원.'

steps.prompt: Test Hajun's rule on the number list: what does the rule say about the blocks 삼 and 사, and does that fit the list?

options.text: They would be the same word, and that fits the list: 삼 = 3 and 사 = 3.
options.reveals: The list does not say that. It gives 삼 = 3 and 사 = 4, two different numbers.

options.text: They would look different in handwriting, but in print they are the same block.
options.reveals: In print too, 삼 and 사 are two different blocks: one has ㅁ at the bottom and one has nothing.

options.text: They would be the same word under the rule, but the list gives 삼 = 3 and 사 = 4, so the rule fails.
The rule does not touch them, because neither block has a bottom letter.
options.reveals: The block 삼 has ㅁ under the vowel. That is exactly the bottom letter the rule is about.

steps.explain: A Hangul block is read as a whole, including the final consonant. If the bottom letter were decoration, 삼 and 사 would be the same word, but the list says 삼 (sam) = 3 and 사 (sa) = 4. So the rule fails; Jiwoo's reading 삼천 원 is the one to check against the payment.
hints: Cover the bottom letter of 삼 with your finger. Which block is left?
Compare that block with the number list. Would the rule still give two different numbers?

steps.prompt: New evidence: Jiwoo pays with a 5,000 won note and the clerk gives her 2,000 won back. Which tag does this support?

options.text: 삼천 원 (3,000 won)
이천 원 (2,000 won)
options.reveals: Then 5,000 - 2,000 = 3,000 would be the change, not 2,000.

options.text: 사천 원 (4,000 won)
options.reveals: Then the change would be 1,000 won.

options.text: 오천 원 (5,000 won)
options.reveals: Then there would be no change.

steps.explain: 5,000 - 2,000 = 3,000. The payment agrees with Jiwoo's reading 삼천 원 and not with Hajun's 사천 원, so the bottom letter did matter.
hints: Work out how much Jiwoo spent: money paid minus change.
Check which of the four tags gives that amount.

steps.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain to Hajun why the bottom letter is not decoration. Use the tag 삼천 원 as your example.

checks.label: mentions the bottom letter / final consonant (받침, ㅁ, ㄴ)
contrasts two blocks with and without a bottom letter (삼/사 or another pair such as 가/간)
does not say the letter is decoration or does not matter

selfAssess: Did I say what the bottom letter does to the block?
Did I show it with a pair of blocks, such as 삼 and 사?

modelAnswers.text: The bottom letter ㅁ is part of the block. Without it the block is 사 (4); with it, it is 삼 (3). So the tag says 3,000 won, not 4,000.
삼 and 사 are different words: 삼 = 3 and 사 = 4. The letter at the bottom changes the number, so it is not decoration.
The letter at the bottom changes the word: 가 and 간 are different words. In the same way 삼 (3) and 사 (4) are different, so the bottom letter matters.

badAnswers.why: Says what the tag says but gives no reason about the bottom letter.

badAnswers.text: The bottom letter is just decoration, so 사천 원 is fine.
badAnswers.why: Repeats Hajun's mistaken claim.

badAnswers.text: The bottom letter doesn't matter, 삼 is 3 and 사 is 4 anyway.
badAnswers.why: Says the letter does not matter, which repeats Hajun's claim.

steps.humanReview: Whether the explanation is clear and addressed to Hajun; other correct examples (for example 가/간 or 바/밤) are accepted by the checks.
hints: Compare 삼 and 사 letter by letter.
Say what the extra letter adds to the block and what number each block means.

rubric.full: Rejects 'decoration' and uses both the tag and the payment as evidence
rubric.partial: Rejects the claim but only with the tag
rubric.none: Accepts 'decoration' or says it cannot be known

rubric.full: Says that the final consonant is part of the block and changes the word, with 3 vs 4
rubric.partial: Mentions the letter but not the effect

alternatives: Other examples, for example 가 / 간 or 바 / 밤, also show that a final consonant changes a word.
Saying 'the block 삼 is sam and the block 사 is sa' is a good explanation in sound terms.
hardCases: A very small final consonant in handwriting may be hard to see; then checking with the money or asking is wise.

cautions.language: All Korean texts are single words or very short phrases. Latin-letter readings follow common revised romanization; other spellings of the same sound (for example k for g) are accepted.
cautions.culture: Prices in Korean markets are often read aloud as well as written, so reading every part of a block saves money; asking the seller to repeat is always polite.
cautions.accessibility: All content is text; numbers are given in Hangul and in digits. Nothing depends on colour or sound.

auto: Choosing the correct reading
Choosing the price that fits the payment
Presence of the bottom-letter and 3/4 contrast, absence of the 'decoration' claim
human: Whether the explanation is clear and respectful to Hajun

subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul: syllable blocks in signs
title: The torn sign over the door
goal: Decide which information is needed to read a half-covered sign, say what you know for sure, and read the final word when more is shown.
thinking: Spotting what two possible words share
Separating what is certain from what is not
Updating after new information
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives a full word to read. Here part of the sign is missing, and you decide which new information could actually separate the two possible words.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul blocks
Knows 화장실 and 화장품 as words
material: A sign above a door in a department store is torn. You can read only the first two blocks: 화장. Two words on this floor begin this way: 화장실 (restroom) and 화장품 (makeup). You want the restroom.

steps.prompt: Which of these would help you tell which word the sign says?

options.text: Reading the first two blocks (화장) again, more slowly.
options.reveals: Both words begin with the same two blocks, 화장, so rereading them cannot separate the words.

options.text: Seeing the block that comes after 화장 on the sign.
The colour of the door.
options.reveals: Colour is not part of the written word; two doors of any colour can carry either word.

options.text: The number of the floor.
options.reveals: The floor tells you where you are, not which of the two words the torn sign shows.

steps.explain: The two words differ only in the third block (실 or 품). The first two blocks are shared, so only the third block can decide.
hints: Write the two possible words under each other and underline what is the same.
Ask which part of the sign could be different between the two words.

steps.prompt: A friend calls and asks: 'What does the sign say?' Answer in one or two short sentences (Korean or English): say what you can read for sure and what you cannot yet.

checks.label: says what is readable (화장)
says what is still unknown

selfAssess: Did I separate the part I can read from the part I cannot?
Did I avoid choosing one word without evidence?

modelAnswers.text: I can read 화장, but I don't know the third block yet. It could be 화장실 or 화장품.
The first two blocks say 화장. I cannot say the whole word until I see the third block.
아직 몰라요. 앞의 두 글자는 화장이에요.
I can read 화장 but not the third block yet; I need to see it to know the word.

badAnswers.why: Chooses one word without evidence and does not say what is unknown.
Does not say what can be read.
Chooses one word as certain and does not say what is unknown.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply is clear to the friend; learners may answer in English.
hints: Say which blocks you can read.
Add what you still need to see before you can name the word.

steps.prompt: The tear is moved and the third block is visible. It is made of ㅍ (top), ㅜ (vowel) and ㅁ (bottom). Which door is it?

options.text: The restroom door (화장실).
options.reveals: The restroom word has the block 실; the letters given make a different block, 품.

options.text: Either one; the first two blocks are enough.
options.reveals: The third block decides between the two words and now it is visible.

options.text: The makeup door (화장품).
Neither; the sign cannot be read.
options.reveals: All three blocks are now readable, so the sign can be read.

steps.explain: The letters ㅍ + ㅜ + ㅁ make the block 품, so the sign says 화장품 (makeup). The restroom is not behind this door.
hints: Put the top letter, the vowel and the bottom letter together into one block.
Compare that block with the two candidate blocks 실 and 품.

rubric.full: Chooses the third block and can explain that the first two blocks are shared
rubric.partial: Chooses it without a reason

rubric.full: Separates what is read for sure from what is not, then reads 품 correctly
rubric.partial: Does one of the two

alternatives: A pictogram (a person symbol) next to the sign would also be good evidence in real life; here only the written word is considered.
hardCases: Other words share the beginning 화장 (for example 화장지, tissue); more than two candidates can exist in a real shop.

cautions.language: All Korean texts are single words or very short phrases. Latin-letter readings follow common revised romanization; other spellings of the same sound (for example k for g) are accepted.
cautions.culture: Signs in Korea often combine a word with a pictogram, but reading the full word is the most reliable way.
cautions.accessibility: The torn sign is described in words; nothing depends on colour or on seeing the picture.

auto: Choice of the deciding block
Choice of the door after the reveal
Presence of a statement of what is known and unknown
human: Whether the reply to the friend is clear

subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul: signs with one or two words, similar blocks
title: A paper on the restaurant wall
goal: Read a covered paper in three steps, do not decide too early, and notice how two look-alike words (있어요, 없어요) change the meaning.
thinking: Waiting for enough evidence
Revising a first guess
Telling two look-alike blocks apart
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives the whole sign at once. Here the paper is uncovered bit by bit and you decide what you can say at each point.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul blocks with final consonants
Knows 있어요 and 없어요
material: A paper is taped to the wall of a restaurant. A hand covers most of it and moves a little each time. Words you may need: 있어요 = there is, 없어요 = there is not.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the answer that fits what you can read so far, then continue.
hints: Use only the letters you can see so far.
Ask yourself what else could start with the same block or the same word.
steps.reflect: A first block rarely tells the whole sign, and a food name alone does not say what the paper says about it. The last word decided the meaning, and it differed from its look-alike by only the bottom letters.

stages.info: You can see only one block: 김

options.text: 김치 (kimchi)
김밥 (rice roll)
I cannot tell yet; more than one word starts with 김.
A name tag: 김 is a common family name.
options.reveals: A family name is one more guess. One block does not show whether it is a name, 김치 or 김밥.

stages.after: 김 starts 김치, 김밥, and also the very common family name 김. One block is too little to decide, so waiting is the reasonable choice.

stages.info: The hand moves. Now you can read the first word: 김치

options.text: The paper is about kimchi, but I do not know what it says about it.
Kimchi is on sale today.
options.reveals: Nothing yet says 'sale'. A paper that names a food can be a menu, a price, a warning or a notice.

options.text: Kimchi is free.
options.reveals: There is no word about free or price yet.

options.text: Kimchi is too spicy.
options.reveals: There is no word about taste yet.

stages.after: You know the topic (kimchi), but not what is said about it. The next word will say that.

stages.info: The hand moves away. The whole paper: 김치 없어요.

options.text: Kimchi is here: 김치 있어요.
options.reveals: The last word has two letters under the vowel (ㅂ and ㅅ), so it is 없어요, not 있어요. The two words look alike but mean opposite things.

options.text: There is no kimchi.
Kimchi is cheap.
options.reveals: Nothing on the paper is about price.

options.text: Please bring kimchi.
options.reveals: The paper does not ask for anything; it states that something is missing.

stages.after: 없어요 (there is not) has the bottom letters ㅂ + ㅅ; 있어요 (there is) has only ㅆ. The paper says there is no kimchi.

steps.prompt: Write what the paper says in your own words (English or Korean). Then name the word that decides the meaning.

checks.label: says there is no kimchi
names the deciding last word

selfAssess: Did I say the meaning, not just the Hangul?
Did I name the word that changes the meaning?

modelAnswers.text: It says there is no kimchi. The last word 없어요 decides it; 있어요 would mean the opposite.
김치 없어요 = no kimchi. The second word, 없어요, is the important one.
They have run out of kimchi. The ending word (없어요) tells me, not the first word.

badAnswers.why: Names only the topic, not what the paper says.
Reads the look-alike word 있어요, the opposite meaning.

steps.humanReview: Whether the learner can tell 있 and 없 apart in handwriting; this needs a person for other fonts.
hints: First say the whole message in English.
Then point to the one word that, if it changed, would flip the message.

steps.prompt: Another paper is covered the same way. You can read 물 and then a covered word that is either 있어요 or 없어요. What must you see before you can say what the paper says?

options.text: The bottom letters of the covered word: one letter (ㅆ) or two (ㅂ + ㅅ).
The first block 물 again, read more slowly.
options.reveals: You can already read 물. Reading it again does not show which of the two last words is covered.

options.text: The colour of the paper.
options.reveals: Colour is not part of the written message.

options.text: Nothing more; 물 alone tells me there is water.
options.reveals: A drink or food name only gives the topic. 있어요 and 없어요 have opposite meanings.

steps.explain: 물 gives the topic only. The two last words look alike and differ in their bottom letters, so you must see those letters to know whether the paper says there is water or there is not.
hints: Write the two possible messages under each other and underline what is different.
Ask which part of the paper could still turn one message into the other.

rubric.full: Waits at stage 1 and does not claim more than the text says at stage 2
rubric.partial: Waits but guesses at stage 2
rubric.none: Names a word at stage 1 as certain

rubric.full: Reads 없어요, states the meaning and names the deciding word
rubric.partial: Reads the meaning without naming the word
rubric.none: Reads 있어요 or the topic only

alternatives: At stage 1 a guess that is marked as a guess is fine in conversation, but this stage rewards waiting because one block fits several words.
Asking the staff after the paper is read is also sensible.
hardCases: In very small print or handwriting, 있 and 없 can look nearly identical; context (is the dish on the table?) then matters.

cautions.language: All Korean texts are single words or very short phrases. Latin-letter readings follow common revised romanization; other spellings of the same sound (for example k for g) are accepted.
cautions.culture: Notices about sold-out items are common on restaurant walls in Korea; 없어요 is a normal, polite way to say an item is not available.
cautions.accessibility: The paper is described in text. Nothing depends on colour, a picture or sound.

auto: Choices at each stage
Presence of the meaning and of the deciding word in the written answer
human: Whether the learner understood the message in their own words

subject: korean
topic: Reading Hangul: look-alike consonants and quiz pairs
title: Make a look-alike quiz for your class
goal: Choose a good look-alike pair, create your own pair of real Korean words, and explain how to tell them apart.
thinking: Setting a condition for a good example
Creating an example that meets it
Explaining a difference in one's own words
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read given words. Here you design the quiz item: it must be a real pair, differ by one letter, and be explainable.
prerequisites: Knows a few simple Hangul words
Can recognize ㅁ/ㅂ, ㅏ/ㅓ, ㄴ/ㄷ shapes
material: Your teacher asks every student to make one look-alike quiz item: two real Korean words that look almost the same, because only one letter is different. Example of the idea: 가 and 나 (one letter different).

steps.prompt: Which pair is a good look-alike quiz item?

options.text: 산 (mountain) and 바다 (sea)
options.reveals: Every block is different; this is not a look-alike pair.

options.text: 물 (water) and 불 (fire)
물 (water) and 물고기 (fish)
options.reveals: One word is inside the other and the lengths differ; this is not a one-letter difference.

options.text: 눈 (snow) and 눈 (eye)
options.reveals: The two words are written exactly the same, so no one can tell them apart by reading.

steps.explain: 물 and 불 are both real words and only the first letter differs (ㅁ vs ㅂ). A good item needs two real words, one small difference, and a difference you can point to.
hints: Write down what stays the same and what changes between the two words in each option.
A good item has a difference you can point to with your finger.

steps.prompt: Make your own pair: write two real Korean words that differ by one letter (a pair that is not printed in this task), and add their English meanings.

checks.label: two Korean words
English meanings given
the two words are not the same word repeated
the two Korean words have the same number of blocks
the pair is your own, not one printed in this task

selfAssess: Are both words real Korean words I know?
Do they differ in exactly one letter?

modelAnswers.text: 달 (moon) - 말 (horse)
공 (ball) / 곰 (bear)
눈 (eye) and 문 (door): the first letter is different.

badAnswers.why: The two words are the same.
No Korean words are written.
Different words with different lengths, not a one-letter difference.
This is the pair printed in the task, not your own.

steps.humanReview: Whether both words are real and really differ by one letter; the checks only see that two words of the same length are written, not the Korean vocabulary.
hints: Think of a word you know well and change one letter of it.
Check that the new block is also a real word.

steps.prompt: Write one or two sentences telling a classmate how to tell your two words apart (which part is different and where).

checks.label: says where the difference is (first, last, top, bottom, vowel, consonant, ...)
names a Korean letter or word

selfAssess: Did I say which part is different?
Could my classmate find it from my sentence?

modelAnswers.text: The first letter is different: ㄷ in 달 and ㅁ in 말. The rest of the block is the same.
Look at the bottom letter: 공 has ㅇ at the bottom and 곰 has ㅁ. The first letter and the vowel ㅗ are the same.

badAnswers.why: Does not say which part differs.
Not related to the task.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is accurate for the learner's own pair and clear to a classmate.
hints: Say which block, and which letter inside it, is different.
Say whether the difference is at the top, in the middle or at the bottom of the block.

rubric.full: Picks 물/불 for a reason and makes two real words that differ by one letter
rubric.partial: Pair is real but differs by more than one letter
rubric.none: Pair is not real or both words are the same

rubric.full: Names the block and the letter that differs and where it is
rubric.partial: Says 'different' only in general

alternatives: Any real pair that differs by one letter is valid, for example 가 / 거, 산 / 삼, 밤 / 밥.
A pair that differs only by sound but looks different (like 김 / 심) can be fine if the written difference is one letter.
hardCases: Some pairs differ by one letter but one word is rare (for example proper names); a person should check that both words are common.

cautions.language: All Korean texts are single words or very short phrases. Latin-letter readings follow common revised romanization; other spellings of the same sound (for example k for g) are accepted.
cautions.culture: Korean has many near-pairs; making your own helps memory. Teachers may prefer pairs from the textbook word list.
cautions.accessibility: All content is text; letters are described by position (top, bottom, left, right), not by colour.

auto: Choosing a good quiz pair
Two Korean words and English meanings present, not repeated
Mentions the differing part
human: Whether both words are real and differ in one letter; whether the explanation fits the pair

subject: korean
topic: Hangul in real life: spelling vs sound of final consonants
title: The sign painter who wrote what he heard
goal: Find the shop signs that copy the sound instead of the spelling, understand why sound alone cannot give the spelling, and write the signs correctly.
thinking: Telling apart what you hear from what is written
Finding errors by checking each line against what you know
Explaining why one sound can come from several written letters
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a final consonant aloud. Here the direction is reversed: from a sound to a spelling, and you see why that direction is unsafe.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul with final consonants (받침)
Knows 꽃, 옷, 신발, 과일, 빵 as vocabulary
material: Dongho paints signs for a market street. A friend read the shop names aloud, and Dongho wrote each one down the way it sounded. Below are six of his signs, with the meaning in English. The words are everyday words you have met in class.

steps.prompt: Some of Dongho's signs are misspelled. Pick one line that has a spelling mistake.
steps.explain: Lines 2 and 4 are misspelled. The flower shop is 꽃 가게 and the clothes shop is 옷 가게. Line 6 is correct: 밥 is written with ㅂ at the bottom, as the word is spelled.
hints: Pick a sign whose word you know from class and spell it from memory. Does its bottom letter match the sign?
Say each sign aloud, then compare the last letter of each word with the word as you know it.

steps.prompt: Dongho wrote his signs by copying what he heard. Why can copying the sound lead to a wrong spelling?

options.text: Only ㄷ can be written at the bottom of a block, so Dongho's signs were right.
options.reveals: Many letters can be written at the bottom (ㅂ in 밥, ㅁ in 삼, ㅅ in 옷). ㄷ is only one of them.

options.text: Bottom letters are never pronounced, so Dongho could not hear them.
options.reveals: Bottom letters are pronounced; the sound is just not always the written letter (옷 is said [옫]).

options.text: Shop signs use a special spelling that is different from ordinary words.
options.reveals: Signs use ordinary spelling. 꽃 is written 꽃 everywhere, on signs and in books.

options.text: Several bottom letters can have the same sound, so the sound alone does not show the spelling.

steps.explain: At the bottom of a syllable, ㅅ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ (and others) are all said like ㄷ. So [꼳] could come from 꽃, and a sound can come from more than one spelling. You must know the written word, not just its sound.
hints: Say the word 꽃 and the word 옷 aloud. Do their last sounds tell you which bottom letter is written?
Ask: if two different letters sound the same, can you tell from the sound which one was written?

steps.prompt: Write the corrected signs in Hangul for the lines that are misspelled.

checks.label: the flower shop uses the written word 꽃
the clothes shop uses the written word 옷
does not keep a sound spelling (꼳, 옫)

selfAssess: Do both signs show the written word, not the sound?
Did I keep the shop word (가게 or 집) after each?

modelAnswers.text: 꽃 가게, 옷 가게
꽃집 / 옷가게
modelAnswers.note: Joined spelling or 집 also works.

modelAnswers.text: 1) 꽃 가게  2) 옷 가게

badAnswers.why: The flower sign still copies the sound.
The clothes sign still copies the sound.
Keeps both mistakes.
Lists the right and the wrong spellings together.

steps.humanReview: Spacing (가게 apart or joined) and whether a learner's own wording of a shop name is natural.
hints: Take the two lines you found and replace only the word with the bottom-letter mistake.
Use the spelling of the word as in your textbook, not the sound in your head.

rubric.full: Picks a wrong line and, in the write step, fixes both
rubric.partial: Fixes only one or picks a correct line (e.g. 닭집)

rubric.criterion: Explaining why sound is not enough
rubric.full: Chooses the reason that several letters share one sound
rubric.partial: Knows the signs are wrong but blames hearing
rubric.none: Thinks signs use a special spelling

alternatives: Writing '꽃집' or '꽃가게' instead of '꽃 가게' is fine.
A learner may spot 닭집 as suspicious; that is a good question, the model answer explains why it is correct.
hardCases: Whether 닭집 is a shop name people really use (it exists; the task only uses it as a spelling check).

cautions.language: The sounds are written in Hangul inside [ ]; this is a way to show sound, not an official spelling. Tense sounds like [빵찝] are not asked.
cautions.culture: Real signs are spelled normally; the 'sign painter' is a made-up situation to practise spelling.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text. Nothing depends on colour or pictures. Romanization is not used.

auto: Which line is picked
Which reason is chosen
Whether both corrected signs contain 꽃 and 옷
human: Spelling and spacing of the learner's own signs

subject: korean
topic: Hangul in real life: bus-stop board
title: Which bus does Hana take today?
goal: Decide which pieces of information on a bus board and in a text are needed to name the right bus, notice the condition printed in brackets, and explain your choice.
thinking: Choosing which information is needed
Noticing a condition hidden in brackets
Combining a board with a message
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a place name on a sign. Here the board has a condition in brackets, and the answer depends on a fact in a different message.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows days of the week (월 ~ 일), numbers + 번
material:
You and your friend Hana are at a bus stop called 시장 앞. Days: 월 Mon, 화 Tue, 수 Wed, 목 Thu, 금 Fri, 토 Sat, 일 Sun. 매일 = every day.

[버스 정류장: 시장 앞]
3번 (월~금): 학교 · 병원
5번 (매일): 공원 · 병원 · 역
7번 (매일): 시장 · 학교

Hana's text: "오늘은 일요일이에요. 병원에 가요. 몇 번 버스예요?"

steps.prompt: To tell Hana the bus number, which pieces of information do you need? Pick all that apply.

options.text: Where Hana wants to go
The name of the stop where you stand
options.reveals: You are already at the stop. The board is the same whatever its name is, so the stop name does not decide the bus.

options.text: What day today is
The lines of the board that list that place
How much the bus costs
options.reveals: The price does not change which bus goes to the place, and the board does not show any price.

steps.explain: You need the place (병원), the board lines that list it, and today's day, because 3번 runs only 월~금. The stop name and the fare do not help choose the number.
hints: First write down what Hana wants to do, then ask which part of the board answers it.
Read what is written in brackets after each bus number. What fact about today would you need to use it?

steps.prompt: Which bus should Hana take today?

options.text: 3번
options.reveals: 3번 goes to 병원, but the bracket says it runs only 월~금, and today is 일요일.

options.text: 7번
options.reveals: 7번 goes to 시장 and 학교. 병원 is not in its list.

options.text: 5번
3번 or 5번, either one
options.reveals: Both list 병원, but 3번 does not run today, so they are not equal.

steps.explain: 5번 lists 병원 and runs 매일. 3번 also lists 병원 but runs only 월~금, and today is Sunday.
hints: Cross out the buses whose list does not name the place.
For the buses that are left, check the bracket against today's day.

steps.prompt: Reply to Hana in English (you may add Korean words): which bus should she take, and why not the other bus that also goes there?

checks.label: names bus 5
refers to the day (Sunday / weekdays / 월~금 / today)
says bus 3 does not run today
does not tell her to take 3

selfAssess: Did I name one bus and say why it works today?
Did I say why the other bus does not work today?

modelAnswers.text: Take bus 5. Bus 3 also goes to the hospital, but it runs only Monday to Friday and today is Sunday.
5번 is the one. 3번 is only 월~금, so it does not run on Sunday.
Hana should take 5. The 3 says Mon-Fri only, but today is 일요일.

badAnswers.text: Take 3 because it goes to the hospital.
badAnswers.why: Ignores the bracket.
Right bus but no reason; the day condition is not mentioned.

badAnswers.text: Take 3, not 5, because it is Sunday.
badAnswers.why: Chooses the bus that does not run today.

badAnswers.text: Take 5. Bus 3 also goes to the hospital but is slower.
badAnswers.why: Gives a reason that is not in the board; the day condition is missing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reason is clear in the learner's own words, including mixed English and Korean.
hints: Say the bus number first, then the reason in one sentence.
Mention the day in today's text and the bracket on the other bus.

rubric.full: Picks the place, the matching board lines and today's day, and leaves out the stop name and the fare
rubric.partial: Misses the day or adds an unneeded item

rubric.full: Chooses 5번 and explains that 3번 runs only 월~금
rubric.partial: Chooses 5번 without a reason

alternatives: Saying '5 or maybe 3 if it runs on Sunday' is not wrong as caution, but the board says 3번 does not run on Sunday.
Naming the bracket as 'Mon to Fri only' or 'not on weekends' are both fine.
hardCases: If the learner is unsure that 월~금 means Monday to Friday, check the day list in the material first.

cautions.language: The Korean is limited to place names, 번 and the days. Hana's text uses only ~이에요, ~에 가요 and 몇 번.
cautions.culture: Some local buses really do change the route on weekends; the board is simplified.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text. The board is shown as plain lines, with nothing depending on colour.

auto: Which items are chosen
Which bus is chosen
Whether the reply names bus 5 and the day condition
human: Whether the written reason is clear

subject: korean
topic: Hangul in real life: reading names and name tags
title: Two name tags, one family?
goal: Read Korean name tags, work out which part is the family name, and revise a guess about how two people are related as new information arrives.
thinking: Separating what a name shows from what it does not show
Revising a judgement with new information
Telling certain from possible
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a name aloud. Here you decide what a name tag really tells you, and what it only suggests.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows 동생 (younger sibling), 저는 ~이에요, ~씨
material: First day of a Korean class. You read the name tags on the desks and listen to people introduce themselves. Korean names are written with the family name first, then the given name. In this class every family name has one syllable (like 박, 김, 이). The tags have no space between them.

steps.prompt: Read each part and choose the statement you are most sure of. Then continue.
hints: Decide using only what you have read so far.
Ask yourself: is this certain, or only possible?
steps.reflect: A name shows the family name and the given name, not whether people are related or whether the person is a boy or a girl. Each new piece of information narrowed what we knew, and we kept 'possible' separate from 'certain'.

stages.info:
Two name tags on the desks:
박지민
박지훈
stages.ask: What can you say for certain?

options.text: They are brother and sister.
options.reveals: Possible, but not certain. 박 is a very common family name, so people with it are often not related.

options.text: They have the same family name.
They have the same given name.
options.reveals: The given names are different (지민 and 지훈).

options.text: They are the same person.
options.reveals: Two tags on two desks. The given names also differ.

stages.after: Both tags start with 박, so the family name is the same. The tags alone do not show whether the two are related.

stages.info: 지훈: 안녕하세요. 저는 지훈이에요. 지민은 제 동생이에요.
stages.ask: Now what do you know about 지민 and 지훈?

options.text: 지민 is 지훈's younger brother or sister.
지민 is 지훈's teacher.
options.reveals: 지훈 says 지민 is 제 동생, 'my younger sibling', not a teacher.

options.text: 지민 is 지훈's older sister.
options.reveals: 동생 means a younger sibling. An older sister would be 누나 or 언니.

options.text: They are classmates only.
options.reveals: 지훈 says 제 동생, so they are family, not just classmates.

stages.after: 지훈 says it directly: 지민 is his younger sibling. So the same family name 박 did fit a family here, but we only learned it from what he said.

stages.ask: Is 지민 a boy or a girl?

options.text: A girl, because 지민 sounds like a girl's name.
options.reveals: The name 지민 is used for both boys and girls, so the name is not evidence.

options.text: A boy, because 지훈 is a boy and they have the same family name.
options.reveals: The family name is shared by everyone in the family and says nothing about being a boy or a girl.

options.text: We do not know yet. Nothing said so far shows it.
A boy, because older siblings are boys.
options.reveals: 지훈 is the older one. Nothing says the older one is a boy, and nothing is said about the younger one.

stages.after: '동생' and the age do not tell the gender, and the name 지민 is used for both. Nothing so far shows whether 지민 is a boy or a girl.

steps.prompt: Now you are 박지민 in your turn to introduce yourself. Write two short lines in Korean (polite speech): say hello, then say your name.

checks.label: a polite greeting (안녕하세요)
says the name 지민 with a polite ending (지민이에요 / 지민입니다)
contains the name 지민
does not use the other name 지훈

selfAssess: Did I say hello and my name in two lines?
Did I put the family name first if I said both parts?

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요. 저는 지민이에요.
안녕하세요? 저는 박지민입니다.
안녕하세요. 제 이름은 박지민이에요.
안녕하세요. 지민이에요.
modelAnswers.note: Also natural: the subject 저는 can be left out.

badAnswers.why: Casual speech; this is a class introduction.
Greeting only; no name.
Says the wrong name (지훈) first.
No polite ending after the name.

steps.humanReview: Whether the introduction sounds natural, and whether the name order is family name first.
hints: Start with the greeting you use in class.
Think about how a name is said politely: which ending follows it, and does your name end in a bottom consonant?

rubric.full: Says that only the shared family name is certain at first and that being siblings is only possible
rubric.partial: Gets the answer but does not notice the difference
rubric.none: Treats the same family name as proof of being family

rubric.full: Updates correctly after 동생 and keeps gender open
rubric.partial: Updates only for the relation
rubric.none: Keeps the first guess against the evidence

alternatives: In stage 1 saying 'they might be siblings' as a possibility is reasonable; only 'for certain' is wrong.
In stage 3 some learners say 'probably a girl'. The task treats 'we do not know yet' as the safe answer.
hardCases: Real names: some Korean family names have two syllables, and 박 is only one of many family names.

cautions.language: Names are only written with Hangul; given names are common and short. 열두 (twelve) is a native Korean number used for age.
cautions.culture: Using family name first is the Korean order. Calling a person by given name + 씨 is common among adults; siblings do not use 씨 to each other.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text. The tags are typed on separate lines in the stage text.

auto: Choices at each stage
Which statements count as reasonable
human: Whether the learner explains the difference between certain and possible

subject: korean
topic: Hangul in real life: a menu board and its notes
title: Mina counts the prices
goal: Judge a friend's claim against the whole menu board, find the line of her reasoning that fails, and explain it using the note under the menu.
thinking: Checking a claim against all the evidence on a page
Finding the first step that fails
Explaining with evidence
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read prices off a menu. Here a note at the bottom changes which price applies, and the claim has to be checked against it.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul and numbers in 천 원
Knows 시 and 분 for time
material:
Mina and you are at a snack shop. Mina looks at the menu board and sends you a text. The board:

[분식집 메뉴]
김밥 3,000원
라면 4,000원
떡볶이 4,000원
※ 점심 세트 (11시~2시) 김밥 + 라면 5,000원
(세트 = set meal)

Mina's text: "지금 12시 30분이에요. 저는 6,000원 있어요. 김밥하고 라면은 7,000원이에요. 못 먹어요."

steps.prompt: Mina says she cannot afford 김밥 + 라면. Look at the whole board and the time in her text. What is the best judgement?

options.text: Mina is right: 3,000 + 4,000 is 7,000, which is more than 6,000.
options.reveals: This uses the single prices only and skips the note at the bottom of the board.

options.text: Mina is wrong: at 12:30 the lunch set gives both for 5,000, less than 6,000.
Mina is right: the set is only for 김밥 and 떡볶이, so 라면 costs extra.
options.reveals: The set line reads 김밥 + 라면. It includes 라면.

options.text: Mina is right: the lunch set ends before 12:30, so the price is 7,000.
options.reveals: The set runs 11시~2시, and 12시 30분 is inside those hours.

steps.explain: 11시~2시 is the lunch set time and 12시 30분 is inside it. 김밥 + 라면 is then 5,000원, so Mina can order both with 6,000원.
hints: Look at every line of the board, not only the prices, before you add anything.
Compare the time in Mina's text with the times written on the board.

steps.prompt: Here is Mina's reasoning, line by line. Pick the FIRST line that is not true at 12:30.
steps.explain: Line 3 is the first line that fails: at 12:30 the set makes 김밥 + 라면 5,000원, not 7,000원. Lines 1, 2 and 4 are true. Line 5 is also false, but only because line 3 was false.
hints: Check the lines one by one from the top and stop at the first one that does not match the board at 12:30.
For each line ask: does the whole board, at that time, agree with it?

steps.prompt: Write a short reply to Mina in English (Korean words are fine) that shows her the board's evidence.

checks.label: mentions the 5,000 won set price
mentions the lunch set or the time
says she can afford / order it
does not simply agree with Mina
does not say she cannot pay
patterns: cannot|can't|can not|not enough|too expensive|not able|못 먹|don't have enough|do not have enough

selfAssess: Does my reply point to the line of the board that Mina missed?
Did I give the new price and compare it to 6,000?

modelAnswers.text: You can order both. It is lunch time now (12:30), and the 점심 set is 김밥 + 라면 for 5,000 won. You have 6,000.
Look at the ※ line: from 11 to 2 the set costs 5,000원, less than your 6,000원, so you can have both.
점심 세트 is 5,000원 until 2시. Now is 12:30, so 김밥 + 라면 is only 5,000 and you have enough.
You are right that separately it is 7,000, but at lunch time the set is 5,000 won, so you can eat both.

badAnswers.why: Agrees with the wrong reading and skips the note.
Repeats the single prices; no set price or time.
Gives the price but not the time condition or whether she can afford it.

badAnswers.text: The set is 5,000 won at lunch time; you cannot afford it.
badAnswers.why: Names the set price but still says she cannot pay.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply is clear and kind, and whether the explanation links the time to the set price.
hints: Start by telling Mina what she can or cannot do, then give the reason.
Say which line of the board you used and what it says about her situation.

rubric.criterion: Using the note on the board
rubric.full: Judges that the lunch set applies at 12:30 and names the 5,000-won price
rubric.partial: Sees the set but not the time condition

rubric.full: Picks the line that states the 7,000-won total
rubric.partial: Picks the conclusion line

alternatives: Saying '5,000 won, so she even has 1,000 left' is a good extension.
Replies that only point to the ※ line and the time, without writing the price, also show the key idea.
hardCases: Is the set offered at exactly 11 or 2? The board does not say; this task uses 12:30 so the case is clear.

cautions.language: The Korean uses numbers in 원, 시 and 분, and 못 먹어요. Prices are written with digits and 원.
cautions.culture: Snack shops (분식집) often have lunch sets with time limits; the board is simplified.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text. The menu is given as plain lines; the ※ mark is read as 'note'.

auto: Choice of the judgement
The failing line
Whether the reply contains the price, the time and not 'Mina is right'
human: Clarity and kindness of the reply

subject: korean
topic: Hangul in real life: final consonants and the sounds you say
title: A rule with exceptions: do you say the bottom letter?
goal: Test a friend's rule about final consonants against real words, produce your own counter-example, and choose a rule that fits all the words.
thinking: Testing a rule against examples
Producing a counter-example
Revising a rule so it fits the facts
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read words with final consonants. Here you test a rule, break it with an example you choose, and repair it.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul with final consonants (받침)
Knows the words 밥, 집, 책, 물, 옷, 꽃, 밖, 맛, 낮
material: Tom, a classmate, has a rule: "The letter at the bottom of a syllable is the sound you say at the end. 밥 is said [밥]. 집 is said [집]." Tom tries it on a list of words. In [ ] is how each word is said.

steps.prompt: Which words break Tom's rule? Pick all that apply.

options.text: 밥 [밥]
options.reveals: The bottom letter ㅂ is said as ㅂ, so the rule holds. It is not a counter-example.

options.text: 옷 [옫]
집 [집]
options.reveals: The bottom letter ㅂ is said as ㅂ, so the rule holds.

options.text: 꽃 [꼳]
물 [물]
options.reveals: The bottom letter ㄹ is said as ㄹ, so the rule holds.

options.text: 밖 [박]

steps.explain: 옷 [옫], 꽃 [꼳] and 밖 [박] are said with a different bottom sound than the written letter (ㅅ, ㅊ and ㄲ). 밥, 집 and 물 follow Tom's rule, so one counter-example is enough to show the rule is not always true.
hints: For each word, compare the bottom letter of the written word with the bottom letter of the sound in [ ].
A word breaks the rule when the two do not match.

steps.prompt: Give ONE more counter-example of your own, a word that is not in the list above. Write the word, how it is said in [ ], and one English sentence saying what happens to the bottom letter. Word bank if you need it: 맛 (taste), 낮 (daytime), 밭 (field).

checks.label: a new word whose bottom letter is not said as written (맛, 낮, 밭, 앞 ...)
shows the sound, for example in [ ] or with →
the sound is not the same as the spelling
says in English or with a letter what the bottom sound becomes

selfAssess: Is my word one where the bottom letter is not said as written?
Did I write the sound in [ ] and say what the bottom sound is?

modelAnswers.text: 맛 [맏] - the bottom letter ㅅ is said like ㄷ, not like ㅅ.
낮 [낟]. The ㅈ at the bottom sounds like d, so it is not said as written.
앞 [압] → the bottom letter ㅍ becomes ㅂ.

badAnswers.why: Gives the sound as the spelling, so it is not a counter-example.
This word follows the rule, so it does not break it.
No word and no sound.

badAnswers.text: 옷 [옫] the bottom letter changes to d
badAnswers.why: 옷 is already in the list; not a new word.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sound given in [ ] is really how the word is said, since the check only looks at surface features.
hints: Pick a word from the bank (or one you know) and say it slowly: what sound do you hear at the very end?
Write the word and its sound in [ ], then check: is the bottom letter in [ ] the same as the written one?

steps.prompt: Now fix Tom's rule. Which new rule fits ALL of the words, including your own counter-example?

options.text: Every bottom letter is said louder and clearer, so ㅅ stays ㅅ and ㅊ stays ㅊ.
options.reveals: This is Tom's rule again. It fails for 옷 [옫] and 꽃 [꼳].

options.text: Every bottom letter is dropped, so 옷 is said [오] and 꽃 is said [꼬].
options.reveals: The bottom letter is still said (as a short stop). 밥 is not said [바].

options.text: Only a few sounds end a syllable: ㅅ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ → ㄷ, ㄲ ㅋ → ㄱ, ㅍ → ㅂ.
Only the words on the list are special; all other words follow the first rule.
options.reveals: The words on the list are only examples. There are many more, so this does not fit them all.

steps.explain: At the bottom of a syllable only a few sounds are used. Letters such as ㅅ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ are said like ㄷ, and ㄲ and ㅋ like ㄱ, ㅍ like ㅂ. The bottom letter is still said, but not always as written.
hints: Check each new rule against 밥 [밥], 옷 [옫], 꽃 [꼳] and 밖 [박].
Reject a rule if a single word from the list breaks it.

rubric.full: Finds exactly 옷, 꽃, 밖 and explains why the others are fine
rubric.partial: Finds some but not all, or marks a fitting word
rubric.none: Cannot compare written and said bottom letters

rubric.full: Gives a real word, its sound in [ ], and what the bottom sound becomes
rubric.partial: Gives a word without the sound or reason
rubric.none: Repeats a word that fits the rule

alternatives: Other valid counter-examples: 앞 [압], 부엌 [부억], 닭 [닥], 값 [갑], 끝 [끋].
A learner may write the sound in Roman letters (e.g. 'mat -> mad'); the surface checks can miss this wording, so human review applies.
hardCases: Some words change further in context (for example before a vowel); the task only asks about the sound at the end of a word.

cautions.language: The sounds are shown in Hangul inside [ ]; the pronunciation of the final sound as a short stop is not explained in detail.

subject: korean
topic: Subject, object and particles: who does what
title: Who teaches whom in the photo?
goal: Decide which captions fit a photo, test your clue on a new caption, and explain why a look-alike caption means the opposite.
thinking: Telling roles by markers, not by position
Using evidence to reject a tempting reading
Explaining a rule to someone who thinks in English word order
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to fill in 이/가 or 을/를 in a given sentence. Here you judge real captions that swap the order of the names, find which clue really decides, and explain the clue.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Has met 이/가 and 을/를 (the doer and the receiver)
material: A class newsletter has a photo: 수진 is teaching 민수 to draw. Five students suggest a caption. Words: 가르쳐요 = teach(es). Particles: 이/가 follow the one who does something; 은/는 follow the topic ("as for ..."); 을/를 follow the one the action is done to.

steps.prompt: In the photo, 수진 is teaching 민수. Which captions describe this photo? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 수진이 민수를 가르쳐요.
민수가 수진을 가르쳐요.
options.reveals: The particle 가 is on 민수, so 민수 is the one who teaches here. That is the opposite of the photo.

options.text: 민수를 수진이 가르쳐요.
수진을 민수가 가르쳐요.
options.reveals: 수진 comes first, but 을 is on 수진: she is the one being taught and 민수 teaches. Word order is not the clue.

options.text: 수진은 민수를 가르쳐요.

steps.explain: In a, c and e, 수진 has 이/가 or 은/는 (the one who does or the topic) and 민수 has 를 (the one who is taught). The order of the two names can change; the particles keep the roles.
hints: Do not read the names from left to right. First find which name has 이/가 or 은/는 and which has 을/를.
Ask of each caption: who has the 를 (or 을) after the name, and is that person taught or teaching?

steps.prompt: A new caption appears: 동생을 엄마가 안아요. (안아요 = hug(s), 엄마 = mom, 동생 = younger sibling.) Who hugs whom?

options.text: 엄마 hugs 동생, because 엄마 has 가 and 동생 has 을.
동생 hugs 엄마, because 동생 is the first name in the sentence.
options.reveals: The first name is not automatically the one who acts. 동생 has 을, so 동생 is the one who is hugged.

options.text: They hug each other, because both names carry a particle.
options.reveals: The two particles are different. 가 marks the one who hugs and 을 marks the one who is hugged.

options.text: We cannot tell, because the names are in an unusual order.
options.reveals: You can tell: the particles keep the roles even when the order changes.

steps.explain: 가 is on 엄마 (the one who hugs) and 을 is on 동생 (the one who is hugged), so the caption means mom hugs her younger sibling. The particles, not the order, give the roles.
hints: Find the particle after each name before you read the order.
Ask which particle marks the one who does the action and which marks the one who receives it.

steps.prompt: A friend reads English word order and says: "수진을 민수가 가르쳐요 starts with 수진, so 수진 teaches." In one or two sentences of English, explain why this caption does NOT fit the photo.

checks.label: mentions the particle (을/를, 이/가) as the clue
says who really teaches / who is taught in this caption (민수 teaches, 수진 is taught)

selfAssess: Did I name the particle that is on 수진?
Did I say who teaches in this caption?

modelAnswers.text: 수진 has the particle 을, so she is the one who is taught; 민수 has 가, so 민수 teaches. Position does not decide it.
The particles show the roles, not the order: 을 marks 수진 as the receiver and 가 marks 민수 as the doer, so it says 민수 teaches 수진.
Because 가 shows that 민수 is the one teaching.

badAnswers.text: Because the order of the words is different from the other captions.
badAnswers.why: Order is not the reason; the particles are.

badAnswers.text: It is wrong because it is a different sentence.
badAnswers.why: No clue named and no role stated.

badAnswers.text: The particle 이 is on 수진, so 수진 teaches 민수.
badAnswers.why: Reverses the roles: 수진 has 을 in the caption.

steps.humanReview: Whether the explanation correctly links each particle with its role, in the learner's own words.
hints: Point to the particle next to 수진 and the particle next to 민수.
Say what each particle tells you about the role of its name.

rubric.full: Picks exactly the three captions where 수진 has 이/은 and 민수 has 를
rubric.partial: Picks two correct captions or one extra

rubric.full: Names the particles and says who teaches in the caption
rubric.partial: Says particles matter but not which one is where

alternatives: Any caption with 수진 as the doer (이/가/은/는) and 민수 with 을/를 fits, in either order.
In spoken Korean 를 may be dropped; the task uses the full written form.
hardCases: Some learners treat 은 in caption e as marking the taught person; it marks the topic, and 를 on 민수 shows the receiver.

cautions.culture: Sentence-final verbs and flexible order of the other parts are standard in Korean; very formal or poetic texts sometimes put the verb elsewhere.

subject: korean
topic: Place particles: 에 (go, be) vs 에서 (do)
title: Where does 민호 do what? A diary check
goal: Find the lines in a short diary where the wrong place-particle is used, say the rule that separates 에 from 에서, and repair the lines.
thinking: Spotting an error by checking each line against a rule
Stating the rule behind a pattern
Repairing without changing the meaning
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives a gap with 에/에서 to fill. Here you scan a whole diary, decide which lines break the rule, and name the rule yourself.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows 에 and 에서 exist (place-particles)
Knows 가요, 있어요, 먹어요, 봐요
material: A learner, 민호, writes his day in Korean. Some place-particles are wrong. Words: 아침 = morning, 점심 = lunch time, 오후 = afternoon, 저녁 = evening, 운동해요 = exercise(s).

steps.prompt: This is 민호's diary about one day. Some lines have a place-particle mistake (there is more than one). Pick any line that has it.
steps.explain: Lines 3, 5 and 7 are wrong: 도서관에서 책을 읽어요 (action at a place), 집에 있어요 (being at a place), 공원에서 운동해요 (action at a place). Lines 1, 2, 4 and 6 are fine.
hints: Underline the verb and the place-particle in each line. Which lines look alike?
Sort the lines into groups by their verb, and see which particle each group uses.

steps.prompt: Which rule explains the difference between 에 and 에서 in this diary?

options.text: 에 shows the place where an action happens; 에서 shows the place someone goes to or is in.
options.reveals: That is reversed. Check 학교에 가요 (go to) and 식당에서 먹어요 (eat at).

options.text: 에 is for big places like a school; 에서 is for small places like a room.
options.reveals: Size does not matter: 학교에서 and 집에서 are both fine for an action.

options.text: 에 and 에서 mean the same; either one works with any verb.
options.reveals: They are different: 도서관에 책을 읽어요 sounds wrong to Koreans.

options.text: 에서 shows the place where an action happens; 에 shows the place someone goes to or is in.

steps.explain: 에서 = the place where you do something (eat, read, study, exercise). 에 = the place you go to, or where someone or something is (가요, 와요, 있어요).
hints: Group the correct lines by their verbs: which verbs go with 에 and which with 에서?
Ask: does the verb say the person moves or stays, or does the person do something there?

steps.prompt: Now rewrite EVERY line that had the mistake, correctly. Write the corrected sentences in Korean and keep the verbs.

checks.label: the library line is corrected (도서관 + 에서 ... 읽어요)
the afternoon line is corrected (집 + 에 ... 있어요)
the park line is corrected (공원 + 에서 ... 운동해요)
does not keep a mistake (도서관에 책 ..., 집에서 있어요, 공원에 운동 ...)

selfAssess: Did I use 에서 for the actions and 에 for being at a place?
Does each sentence still end politely?

modelAnswers.text: 도서관에서 책을 읽어요. 오후에 집에 있어요. 저녁에 공원에서 운동해요.
도서관에서 책을 읽어요. 집에 있어요. 공원에서 운동해요.
도서관에 가서 책을 읽어요. 오후에 집에 있어요. 공원에 가서 운동해요.
modelAnswers.note: Also fine: the place is a destination, then the action follows.

badAnswers.text: 도서관에 책을 읽어요. 오후에 집에 있어요. 공원에서 운동해요.
badAnswers.why: Line 3 still has the mistake.

badAnswers.text: 도서관에서 책을 읽어요. 오후에 집에서 있어요. 공원에서 운동해요.
badAnswers.why: Line 5 still has the mistake.

badAnswers.text: 도서관에서 책을 읽어요. 오후에 집에 있어요. 공원에 운동해요.
badAnswers.why: Line 7 still has the mistake.

badAnswers.text: 도서관에서 노래해요. 집에 있어요. 공원에서 잠자요.
badAnswers.why: The verbs were changed instead of repairing the particles.
Not a full repair: lines are missing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the learner's rewrite stays natural if the learner changes the verbs or adds words.
hints: For each wrong line decide: does the person go or stay there, or do something there?
Read your sentence aloud: is the person doing something at the place, or going or being there?

rubric.full: Picks a wrong line and can say why (action at a place)
rubric.partial: Picks a wrong line without a reason

rubric.full: All three lines are repaired with the right particle and stay polite
rubric.partial: One or two lines repaired

alternatives: Some sentences with a movement first (도서관에 가서 읽어요) are also correct.
Dropping 을/를 in speech (책 읽어요) is common and not an error for this task.
hardCases: 학교에서 가요 (go from school) is possible with another meaning; this task uses the basic pattern.

cautions.language: Only 에 and 에서 and short present-tense sentences. 아침에, 점심에 use 에 for time; this is not asked.
cautions.culture: Diaries are normally written in plain style (-ㄴ다); the task uses polite -요 to stay at level 1.

subject: korean
topic: Time and place: who is where, when
title: Can 지나 and 톰 meet at the library?
goal: Pick the facts that matter for a meeting (a place AND a time for both people), decide with them, and propose a repair in Korean.
thinking: Sufficiency of information
Combining place and time conditions
Ignoring facts that do not matter
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks where one person goes. Here two messages each look fine alone, and you must find which facts to combine, notice that the times do not match, and propose a fix.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows 에 (going, being) and 에서 (doing) at a basic level
Knows 오전 and 오후
material:
Two messages for tomorrow. 오전 = morning (a.m.), 오후 = afternoon (p.m.), 저녁 = evening, 시장 = market, 집 = home.

지나: 저는 내일 오전에 도서관에서 한국어를 공부해요. 오후에는 시장에 가요.
톰: 저는 내일 오전에 집에 있어요. 오후에는 도서관에 가요. 저녁에 친구를 만나요.

steps.prompt: 지나 wants to study with 톰 at the library tomorrow, in the morning or in the afternoon. Which facts do you need to know whether this can work? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Where 톰 is in the afternoon.
Where 지나 is in the evening.
options.reveals: The question is only about the morning or the afternoon; the evening is not part of it.

options.text: Where 지나 is in the morning.
Where 톰 is in the morning.
Where 지나 is in the afternoon.
Where 톰 is in the evening.
options.reveals: The question is only about the morning or the afternoon; the evening is not part of it.

steps.explain: To compare you need each person's place for each time of day in question: 지나 morning and afternoon, 톰 morning and afternoon. The evening does not matter for this plan.
hints: Re-read the question: which people and which times of day does it mention?
For each option ask: would knowing this change my decision about meeting?

steps.prompt: Now decide: can 지나 and 톰 study together at the library tomorrow, as the messages stand?

options.text: No. 톰 does not go to the library tomorrow.
options.reveals: 톰 says 오후에는 도서관에 가요, so he does go to the library.

options.text: No. They are at the library at different times of the day.
Yes. Both of them go to the library tomorrow.
options.reveals: Both name the library, but at different times of the day. Check 오전 and 오후.

options.text: Yes. Both of them are at the library in the morning.
options.reveals: 톰 is at home (집에 있어요) in the morning.

steps.explain: 지나 is at the library in the morning (도서관에서 공부해요) and goes to the market in the afternoon. 톰 is at home in the morning and goes to the library in the afternoon. Both are at the library tomorrow, but never at the same time.
hints: Fill a small table: person, morning place, afternoon place.
Check each option against your table, one by one.

steps.prompt: Write a short message in Korean from 지나 to 톰 (polite -요) that proposes a time (오전 or 오후) to study together at the library.

checks.label: names the library (도서관)
names a time (오전, 오후, a clock time ...)
polite sentence ending (…해요, …까요, …어요)
proposes or asks (같이, 함께, a question, 어때요 ...)

selfAssess: Does my time really work for both of us (one of us has to change a plan)?
Did I use 에 for the time and for going to the library?

modelAnswers.text: 톰 씨, 내일 오전에 도서관에 와요? 같이 공부해요.
내일 오후에 같이 도서관에서 공부해요. 저는 시장에 안 가요.
톰 씨, 오전에 도서관에서 만나요. 괜찮아요?

badAnswers.why: No time and no proposal.
The library is not named and nothing is proposed.
A statement about herself; it does not propose or ask anything.
Only words; no sentence.

steps.humanReview: Whether the proposal is clear and natural, and whether the learner noticed that someone has to change a plan.
hints: Choose a time of day where one of the two could change his or her plan.
Name the time, the place, and end with a request to study together.

rubric.full: Chooses the four place-and-time facts and leaves out the two others
rubric.partial: Chooses all four but also one extra, or misses one

rubric.full: Library, time and a request; polite
rubric.partial: One element missing

alternatives: Either 지나 or 톰 can change; the message may ask either of them.
A clock time such as 두 시에 is also acceptable.
hardCases: Some learners say "yes" because both go to the library; the times are what decide.

cautions.language: Only simple present-tense sentences. 한국어를 공부해요 is the object of studying.
cautions.culture: Using 씨 after a name is polite among adults; it is optional in the answer.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; the photo or scene is described in words, nothing depends on colour. Romanization is not provided.

The yes/no decision
Surface check that the message names the library and a time
human: Whether the proposal is natural and sensible

subject: korean
topic: Sentence parts: doer, place, thing
title: Make a sentence card: who, where, what
goal: Use the roles of doer, place and thing (with their particles) to build your own correct sentence, and check other cards against the same rules.
thinking: Building a sentence from roles
Checking against explicit rules
Finding a role swap that looks fine at a glance
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives a sentence with gaps. Here you apply four rules, make your own sentence, and then use the same rules as a checker.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Has met 이/가, 을/를, 에서
Knows 먹어요 and 마셔요
material: A game with sentence cards. Words: 동생 = younger sibling, 공원 = park, 빵 = bread, 카페 = cafe, 식당 = restaurant, 시장 = market, 사요 = buy(s), 읽어요 = read(s).

steps.prompt: A game of sentence cards has four rules: (1) the doer + 이/가 or 은/는, (2) the place + 에서, (3) the thing + 을/를, (4) the verb at the end. Which sentences follow all four rules? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 동생이 공원에서 빵 먹어요.
options.reveals: The thing (빵) has no 을/를. Spoken Korean often drops it, but the card rules ask for it.

options.text: 동생을 공원에서 빵이 먹어요.
options.reveals: The particles are swapped: this says that the bread eats the sibling.

options.text: 동생이 빵을 공원에서 먹어요.
동생이 공원에 빵을 먹어요.
options.reveals: 공원에 marks a place you go to; for the place where you eat, the card needs 에서.

options.text: 동생이 공원에서 빵을 먹어요.

steps.explain: c and e have all four parts: doer 동생이, place 공원에서, thing 빵을, verb 먹어요 at the end. The order of the middle parts can change; the verb stays last.
hints: Check one rule at a time. Underline the particle on each part.

steps.prompt: Make your own card. Write one Korean sentence about someone (you, a friend, your family) who eats or drinks something at a place. Follow all four rules, and end the verb with -아요/어요.

checks.label: has a doer with 이/가 or 은/는 (저는, 친구가, 엄마는 ...)
has a place with 에서
has a thing with 을/를
ends with a polite verb (-아요/어요)
the verb is eat or drink (먹어요, 마셔요 ...)
the roles are not swapped (no person with 을/를, no food or drink with 이/가)

동생이 식당에서 밥을 먹어요.
엄마가 빵을 집에서 먹어요.

에 instead of 에서.
No 을/를 on the thing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is natural: the chosen thing and verb fit, and the learner did not only copy the examples.
hints: Decide the three parts first: who, where, what.

steps.prompt: Your classmate made four cards. One card has the wrong particles, so the roles are mixed up. Pick it.
steps.explain: Line 3 says that the book reads the sibling: 이 is on 책 and 를 is on 동생. Written correctly: 동생이 책을 읽어요.
hints: Read each card by asking: who does it, and what is it done to?
Is the doer someone who can really do the action?

rubric.partial: Picks one and no wrong one
rubric.none: Picks sentences with swapped or missing particles

rubric.full: Doer, place with 에서, thing with 을/를, polite verb last

Other eating and drinking verbs, places and things are fine.
hardCases: Someone may write 저도 or 우리는 as the doer; both are fine.

cautions.culture: Eating and drinking in a cafe or restaurant is typical; foods are everyday ones.

subject: korean
topic: Who does the action: reading the verb and the particles
title: Who eats the cake? The chat keeps changing
goal: Revise your idea of who does the action as a chat adds one sentence at a time, separate what is stated from what is only suggested, and write a negative sentence with the right roles.
thinking: Updating a judgement with new evidence
Stated vs suggested (claim vs evidence)
Reading the verb before deciding who does what
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives a single sentence and one question. Here the same family scene grows in three parts and you must keep revising what you can really say.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Has met 이/가, 은/는, 을/를
Knows 안 + verb
material: A family chat about a cake: Mom (엄마), Dad (아빠), a younger sibling (동생) and the speaker (저). The sentences arrive in three parts.

steps.prompt: Read the family chat one part at a time. Words: 만들어요 = make(s), 좋아해요 = like(s), 먹어요 = eat(s), 안 + verb = does not. Choose the reading that fits what you have read so far.

options.text: 엄마 eats it, because she makes it.
options.reveals: 만들어요 says who makes it. Making and eating are different actions.

options.text: We cannot tell yet; we only know who makes it.
Probably 엄마 eats it too, since people often eat what they make.
options.reveals: That is a guess from a habit. The sentence only says that 엄마 makes it.

options.text: 동생 eats it, because it is for children.
options.reveals: Nothing in the sentence mentions 동생 or children.

stages.after: The sentence has a doer (엄마가) and a thing (케이크를), but the verb is 만들어요: it tells who makes the cake, not who eats it.

stages.ask: Who will probably eat the cake now?

options.text: 동생 probably eats it, since 동생 likes it.
동생 makes it, because 동생이 comes first.
options.reveals: 엄마가 was the one who makes it. 동생이 goes with 좋아해요 (likes).

options.text: Only 엄마 eats it, because she makes it.
options.reveals: The new sentence is about 동생, not about 엄마.

options.text: 동생 surely eats it, because 좋아해요 means eats.
options.reveals: 좋아해요 means likes. Liking a cake is a good sign, but it is not the same as eating.

stages.after: 좋아해요 means likes. It is a good sign that 동생 will eat the cake, but it is not proof.

stages.info: 아빠는 케이크를 안 먹어요. 저는 케이크를 먹어요.

options.text: Only 동생 eats it; 저 and 아빠 do not.
options.reveals: 저는 케이크를 먹어요 says that the speaker eats it.

options.text: 아빠 and 저 eat it; 동생 does not.
options.reveals: 안 comes before 먹어요: 아빠 does NOT eat it.

options.text: Probably 아빠 eats it and 저 does not.
options.reveals: The two sentences say the opposite: 아빠 does not eat it and 저 does.

options.text: 저 eats it and 아빠 does not; 동생 is only likely.

stages.after: 안 + verb = does not. 아빠 does not eat it, 저 does, and 동생 probably does. 엄마 is still not mentioned as an eater.

steps.reflect: Each new sentence changed the answer. At first nothing was known about the eater; then a likely eater appeared; then one person was ruled out. Check which verb you are reading before you decide who does it.
hints: Decide using only the parts you have read so far.

title: A friend's list for the convenience store

thinking: Satisfying several conditions at once

material:
Your friend texts you before you go to the convenience store:

"편의점에 가요? 부탁해요!
칠천오백 원 있어요.
물 두 개 사요.

빵 한 개: 천 원

김밥 두 개: 사천 원
김밥 세 개: 사천오백 원
김밥 네 개: 육천 원

(The text says: your friend has 7,500 won, buys 2 bottles of water, wants gimbap and bread too, and buys 7 things in all.)

steps.prompt: Look at the gimbap lines of the price list. Which statement is true?

options.text: Gimbap is cheaper per piece when you buy more: 3 cost 4,500 won.
Each gimbap costs 2,000 won, so 3 gimbap cost 6,000 won.
options.reveals: The list says 세 개: 사천오백 원, so 3 gimbap cost 4,500 won, not 6,000.

options.text: Gimbap gets more expensive: 4 gimbap cost 8,000 won.
options.reveals: The list says 네 개: 육천 원, so 4 gimbap cost 6,000 won.

options.text: Two gimbap cost 3,000 won, one cheaper than 1 + 1.
options.reveals: The list says 두 개: 사천 원, so 2 gimbap cost 4,000 won.

steps.explain: The table lists the price of the whole set: 1 gimbap 2,000, 2 gimbap 4,000, 3 gimbap 4,500, 4 gimbap 6,000. The price is not always 2,000 times the number.
hints: Read each gimbap line as 'number of gimbap: price of all of them'.
Compare the price of each number of gimbap with the price of one gimbap.

steps.prompt: Find 2 different baskets that fit EVERYTHING in the text. g = number of gimbap, b = number of bread (the 2 bottles of water are already fixed).

constraints.ok: Both gimbap and bread are included.
constraints.fail: 김밥하고 빵도 사요: buy at least one of each.

constraints.ok: Seven things in all with the 2 bottles of water.
constraints.fail: 모두 일곱 개: with the 2 bottles of water, gimbap plus bread must be 5.
More than 7,500 won (칠천오백 원). Remember water costs 1,000 won in all and use the price LIST for gimbap.

steps.explain: There are exactly two baskets: 1 gimbap + 4 bread (water 1,000 + 2,000 + 4,000 = 7,000 won) and 3 gimbap + 2 bread (1,000 + 4,500 + 2,000 = 7,500 won). 2 gimbap + 3 bread costs 8,000 and 4 gimbap + 1 bread costs 8,000, which is too much. hints: Write the conditions in your own words first: how much money, how many things in all, what must be included.
Count the 2 bottles of water too. Then try the possible numbers of gimbap one at a time.
For each try add water, gimbap (from the LIST) and bread, then compare with 7,500 won.

gives the gimbap count
gives the bread count
says the total price (원)
counts with 개 use native numbers (한 개, 세 개 ...), not 삼 개
the counts and the total fit one valid basket

badAnswers.why: No items, counts or price.

badAnswers.text: 김밥 두 개, 빵 세 개 샀어요. 팔천 원이에요.
badAnswers.why: This basket costs 8,000 won, more than the money.

rubric.partial: Builds one valid basket, or treats gimbap as 2,000 each

topic: Two number systems and counting words
title: Can 일, 이, 삼 do everything?
goal: Test a learner's rule that Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼) work everywhere, state the real pattern, and write your own two sentences that show it.
thinking: Finding counter-examples to a rule
Stating a rule that fits all the evidence
Making your own examples
differsFromPlain: Plain practice drills one list of numbers. Here you test a tempting rule against real sentences, find which ones break it, and make your own examples.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows 하나 둘 셋 / 한 두 세 and 일 이 삼
Has met the words 개, 명, 살, 시, 원, 분, 월, 일, 번
material:
Tom is learning Korean. He says: "I know 일, 이, 삼, 사, 오 ... so I will use only these numbers for everything!"

Here are six sentences Tom wrote:

steps.prompt: Which of Tom's sentences would sound wrong to a Korean person? Select every one.

options.text: 의자 이 개 있어요.
이만 원이에요.
options.reveals: This is correct: money uses Sino numbers (이만 원 = 20,000 won).

options.text: 동생이 오 살이에요.
오늘은 오월 오 일이에요.
options.reveals: This is correct: months and days use Sino numbers (5월 5일).

options.text: 학생이 오 명 있어요.
삼 번 버스예요.
options.reveals: This is correct: bus and route numbers use Sino numbers.

steps.explain: Three sentences are wrong because 개 (things), 살 (age) and 명 (people) need native numbers: 의자 두 개, 다섯 살, 학생이 다섯 명. The other three are fine: money (원), dates (월, 일) and numbers like bus 3 use Sino numbers.
hints: Say the six sentences aloud one by one. Which ones have you heard in real life with a Sino number, and which with a native one?
Say each sentence in your head. Which ones have you heard with 하나, 둘, 셋 style numbers instead?

steps.prompt: Which rule fits ALL six sentences?

options.text: Both kinds of numbers are always fine; the speaker chooses freely.
options.reveals: Three of the sentences sound wrong, so the choice is not free.

options.text: The word you are counting decides which number system fits.
Small numbers are native (하나, 둘 ...) and big numbers are Sino (이십오, 이만 ...).
options.reveals: 오월 오 일 uses the small number 5 as Sino, and 이십오 살 is big but needs the native 스물다섯, so size does not decide.

options.text: Native numbers are for casual speech and Sino numbers for polite speech.
options.reveals: The same numbers appear in polite speech: 세 개 주세요 and 이만 원이에요 are both polite.

steps.explain: The counting word decides. Things, people, age and hours (개, 명, 살, 시) use native numbers; money, minutes, months, days and numbers like bus 3 (원, 분, 월, 일, 번) use Sino numbers.
hints: Make two columns: the wrong sentences and the right ones. What stays the same inside each column?
Test each rule against a sentence it should explain. Does it also explain the others?

steps.prompt: Show Tom the pattern with your OWN two Korean sentences (write numbers in Hangul): one with a native number and 개, 명, 살 or 시; one with a Sino number and 원, 분, 월, 일 or 번.
